title: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 3.9 Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions
intro: After this lesson you can describe the sampling distribution of $\hat p_1-\hat p_2$: its mean, standard deviation and shape, check the conditions for two independent samples, and find probabilities with a $z$ score.

moments.title: Sampling distribution
moments.text: A model of all possible values of a statistic from samples of size $n$ from the same population.

moments.title: Two populations, one categorical variable
moments.text: Take one sample from each population and look at $\hat p_1-\hat p_2$.

moments.title: The sign of the difference
moments.text: Positive means the sample from population 1 had the larger proportion. Negative means population 2 did.

moments.title: What the model needs
moments.text: The two population proportions and the two sample sizes.

moments.title: Random samples for the center
moments.text: Without random samples the center is not trustworthy.

moments.title: Standard deviation
moments.text: $\sigma_{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}=\sqrt{\dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}$. It is on the formula sheet.

moments.title: Check independence twice
moments.text: Each sample is at most 10% of its own population.

moments.title: Check normality for both samples
moments.text: Expected successes and failures are each at least 10 in both samples.

moments.title: Normal model centered at the true difference
moments.text: Most sample differences sit near the true difference.

moments.title: Adults and teenagers on Netflix
moments.text: 62% of adults and 55% of teens, with $n_1=200$ and $n_2=150$.

moments.title: At least equals more than
moments.text: A normal model gives a single value probability 0, so $\ge$ and $>$ give the same answer.

moments.title: Urban and rural vaccine willingness
moments.text: 78% of 250 urban and 70% of 300 rural residents. The mean is 0.08.

moments.title: Rural sample larger
moments.text: The event is $\hat p_U-\hat p_R<0$. $z=-2.149$ and the probability is about 0.0158.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video checks the counts with the population proportions. For this sampling distribution the proportions $p_1$ and $p_2$ are given. Later, when they are unknown, you use sample counts or a pooled proportion.

sections.title: Describe the model and find a probability
sections.intro: Name the statistic with a direction, check the conditions for both samples, then find center, spread and shape. A $z$ score and a normal probability finish the job.
steps: State the difference, for example $\hat p_A-\hat p_T$, so you know which sign means which sample.
Check randomization, the 10% condition for each sample, and large counts for each sample.
Mean $=p_1-p_2$. Standard deviation from the formula.
Shape is approximately normal. Standardize: $z=(x-\mu)/\sigma$, then find the area.

traps.title: Describe the sampling distribution fully
traps.better: The sampling distribution of $\hat p_A-\hat p_T$ is approximately normal with mean 0.07 and standard deviation about 0.0532, because both samples are random, each is under 10% of its population, and all expected counts are at least 10.

traps.title: Checking conditions for one sample only
traps.weak: 200 is less than 10% of all adults, so independence is met.
traps.better: Check both samples: 200 adults is under 10% of all adults and 150 teens is under 10% of all teens.

traps.title: Subtracting the standard deviations
traps.better: Add the variances under one square root, even though the means are subtracted. Variability from each sample adds.

traps.title: Sign errors in the direction
traps.weak: The rural sample is bigger, so we want $\hat p_U-\hat p_R>0$.
traps.better: A larger rural proportion makes $\hat p_U-\hat p_R$ negative, so the event is $\hat p_U-\hat p_R<0$.

traps.title: Probability statement missing
traps.better: $P(\hat p_A-\hat p_T>0.10)\approx0.286$. About 28.6% of all possible differences in sample proportions exceed 10 percentage points.

questions.stem: Population 1 has $p_1=0.40$ and population 2 has $p_2=0.30$. Independent random samples have $n_1=100$ and $n_2=150$. What is the mean of the sampling distribution of $\hat p_1-\hat p_2$?
why: Correct. The mean is the true difference, $0.40-0.30=0.10$.
This is the average of the two proportions.
The mean does not depend on the sample sizes.

questions.stem: Using the same populations and samples, which expression gives the standard deviation?
why: This is the variance because the square root is missing.
Variances add, so the sign is plus.
Adding standard deviations is not correct.

questions.stem: Which condition must be checked for both samples when finding the sampling distribution of $\hat p_1-\hat p_2$?
opts: The samples come from the same population
Each sample is less than or equal to 10% of its population
The two samples have the same size
The two population proportions are equal
why: The samples come from two different populations.
Correct. Check the 10% condition separately for each sample.
The sample sizes do not have to match.
If they were equal the true difference would be 0, which is not required.

questions.stem: In the Netflix example, $\mu=0.07$ and $\sigma=0.0532$. Which expression gives the $z$ score for a difference of 0.10?
why: This reverses the order of subtraction, giving the wrong sign.
This forgets to subtract the mean.
Adding the mean is not standardizing.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: In one district, 30% of students at School A and 24% of students at School B use public transport. A random sample of 180 students from School A and an independent random sample of 160 from School B are taken. Let $\hat p_A-\hat p_B$ be the difference in sample proportions.
parts: (a) Verify that the normal model is appropriate. Assume each school has more than 1,800 students.
(b) Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\hat p_A-\hat p_B$.
(c) Find the probability that the sample proportion for School A exceeds the sample proportion for School B by at least 0.10.
sample: (a) Both samples are random and independent. 180 and 160 are under 10% of each school. Expected counts: School A, 54 and 126; School B, 38.4 and 121.6. All are at least 10, so the distribution is approximately normal.
(d) About 20.2% of all possible pairs of samples would give an A proportion at least 0.10 above the B proportion.

flags.text: The video checks normality using the population proportions. The CED condition is stated for sample counts; the page uses the population proportions because they are given, and notes how that changes later.
The video rounds the standard deviation to 0.0372 and reports z = -2.151 and P = 0.0157. Unrounded, z = -2.149 and P = 0.0158; the page uses the unrounded values.
